nodes.title: Objective Mutual Assent
nodes.conceptSummary:
A valid contract requires mutual assent, manifested through an objective offer and an unequivocal acceptance.
The core invariant is the objective theory of contracts: assent is judged by a reasonable person's outward manifestation, not hidden subjective intent. A revocation is only effective when communicated to the offeree before acceptance.

nodes.title: Consideration and Bargained-for Exchange
nodes.conceptSummary:
Enforceable promises require consideration: a bargained-for exchange of legal value.
The fundamental invariant is mutuality of obligation. Past consideration or moral obligation does not constitute legal consideration unless promissory estoppel applies to prevent manifest injustice.

conceptualVariants.content: The fundamental invariant is mutuality of obligation.

nodes.title: Material Breach and Constructive Conditions
nodes.conceptSummary:
When one party commits a material breach, the non-breaching party's constructive duties under the contract are suspended.
The core invariant is substantial performance: if a breach is minor and immaterial, the non-breaching party must still perform their obligations and may only sue for damages, rather than terminating the contract.

conceptualVariants.content: The core invariant is substantial performance: if a breach is minor and immaterial, the non-breaching party must still perform their obligations and may only sue for damages, rather than terminating the contract.

proceduralPerturbations.probe: If boundary inputs invert, how does Material Breach and Constructive Conditions preserve state?
proceduralPerturbations.expectedBoundaryBehavior: "Cannot terminate: under the doctrine of substantial performance (Jacob & Youngs v. Kent), an immaterial breach only entitles the owner to difference-in-value damages, not contract forfeiture."
